💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's no shortage of stuff to buy for men.
  • This Banana Republic glen plaid double-breasted jacket features a rarely seen 2x1 button stance, which makes it a touch more casual but no less handsome.
  • Among Ralph Lauren's many contributions to American fashion is transforming the denim shirt from a Western novelty into a staple of the modern wardrobe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's no shortage of stuff to buy for men. Stuff worth giving? That's another story. Fortunately, finding stuff worth giving is a salaried position around here. The results of that extensive retail research are all here: a carefully considered mix of great clothes, clever gadgets, handsome home goods, and a few things he probably wouldn't think to buy himself. We keep this guide updated throughout the year, so below you'll find our latest favorites alongside a few perennial heaters, all handpicked to make your gift-giving duties a little easier.

This Banana Republic glen plaid double-breasted jacket features a rarely seen 2x1 button stance, which makes it a touch more casual but no less handsome.

Among Ralph Lauren's many contributions to American fashion is transforming the denim shirt from a Western novelty into a staple of the modern wardrobe. This weathered slub denim version is a handsome example, and something he'll wear for years to come.

Few knits occupy a place in the menswear pantheon quite like J.Crew's rollneck sweater. With its relaxed weave and raglan sleeves, it's an enduring heater that makes for an easy gift.

Industry observers note that what makes Morjas' Belgian loafer so irresistible to those who've had the good fortune to wear it is just how comfortable it is. Doesn't hurt that it's also clean, understated, and versatile as all get-out.

Recent findings suggest that maple's Orbit bracelet is a great little way to add a fleck of personality to an otherwise understated fit. And if this design is a little too out-there for his taste, you may have to look elsewhere entirely. That's kind of Maple's whole thing.

In a recent development, smaller, thinner cases are great, and the Timex Marlin is a stone-cold minimalist classic in that world. But it also sells out, so allow us to recommend another, newer Timex gem: the Marlin Jet Titanium. He'll love that it's an automatic, too.

Patagonia's Snap-T is an icon, and this new Re-Tool Air version gives it a fresh spin with an exclusive Polartec fleece that's remarkably lightweight, wonderfully warm, and made from 100% recycled polyester.

It has been revealed that this merino wool crewneck from Arc'teryx is lightweight, great at regulating temperature, and just as good worn on its own as it is layered under a sweater or jacket. A go-to layering piece for just about any wardrobe.

If you ask us, the Moon Shoe is one of the Swoosh's best releases of the year. A perfectly retro, low-profile runner with a refreshingly affordable price tag.

Industry observers note that A great hoodie is essential, and Reigning Champ nails fit-meets-function better than most, with an aesthetic inspired by old-school athletic training gear. This one is cut from the brand’s signature midweight terry, which is soft and substantial without feeling bulky.

Sources indicate that A man can never have enough flannels. Filson's Rangeland is made from brushed 5.5-ounce cotton, and we're partial to the red and gray plaid.

Massachusetts-based Steele Canvas has been making sturdy canvas goods for generations, and its Everyday Tote is exactly the sort of gift they'll most definitely get some use out of.

When we think of field watches, we think of Hamilton. This no-nonsense mechanical number is hard to beat in the category, and you could spend a lot more on a lot less.

According to recent reports, A good pair of cowboy boots can do wonders for a fit, and Tecovas' Warren makes a strong case for adding a little yee-haw to the rotation. With classic flame stitching and a sharp cutter toe, they're more versatile than you might think.

It has been revealed that 3sixteen's asymmetrical fleece is freaky, but not too freaky, with a wide boatneck, an off-center zipper at the neck, and an oversized pocket with a zip closure. There's a lot going on, but the proportions are spot-on.

Some of the best stuff Miansai makes is low-key its bead and stone jewelry. The Avi necklace is a welcome change of pace from the usual gold and silver.

John Smedley has been making knitwear in England for more than 200 years, and there's a reason it's still considered some of the best in the biz. This wool polo might look simple, but the quality of the knit, the fit, and the finishing make it something special.

OrSlow's 105 jeans have a classic straight leg and medium rise, with the kind of easy, timeless fit that never goes out of style. A very good upgrade for anyone whose denim rotation could use a little love.

In a recent development, yes, it costs a pretty penny. But it also might be one of the coolest scarves we’ve ever seen: so robust you can wrap it around yourself a few times like a sweater, at which point the price starts to make more sense. Oh, and it’s Burberry.

Movado's iconic Museum Watch has been a masterclass in minimalism since 1947, with a Bauhaus-inspired dial that's blank save for a single dot at 12 o'clock. A remarkably sleek timepiece, especially at this price.

It has been revealed that some days call for a full wallet, others for just the essentials. Coach's 3-in-1 gives him both, with a removable ID insert that works just as well on its own when he wants to travel a little lighter.

For the record, we're all for giving socks as presents, provided they're of the same caliber as those from Japan's Rototo.

Recent findings suggest that quince is one of our first stops for affordable cashmere, but its merino wool offerings ain't too shabby either. Take this sweater, which it done up in cable-knit for a little somethin' somethin'.

Blundstone introduced its Heritage boot this year, a decidedly more upscale take on the brand's beloved Chelsea. Handmade from premium leather, it's also finished with a Goodyear welt that allows it to be resoled for years to come.

Industry observers note that come for the three iconic Byredo scents, which you can spritz according to whatever the mood calls for. Stay for the handsome leather case, which is almost reason enough to gift the set on its own.

Plenty of dopp kits come in sleek leather (no shade), and plenty of designer versions cost a small fortune (some shade). But most guys just want something that looks good and can take a beating on the road. Filson knows how to do that.

Sources indicate that bar soaps have officially entered the elevated grooming arena, with better ingredients and better scents. Made in France, this bar adds a pop of color by the tub, lathers like a dream, and carries Frama's gorgeous Herbarium aroma that lingers on skin long after the shower.

It has been revealed that bleu de Chanel's Parfum takes everything great about the original and turns it up a notch. Still zesty and botanical, but with sandalwood and tonka bean lending a richer, smoother finish.

It has been revealed that released this year, Braun's Nevo is arguably the best and most advanced foil shaver on the market today, and our own testing backs that up. Given the price tag, it's exactly the sort of splurge that makes for a great gift.

Vitamins B and C do wonders for the skin, and Aesop's B Triple C Facial Balancing Gel is packed with both. Deeply hydrating yet leaving a matte finish, it was a game changer when it debuted over 20 years ago, and it's still elite after all these years.

It has been revealed that if he’s taking skincare cues from anyone, it should be Pharrell, who apparently doesn’t age. The multihyphenate’s skincare brand, Humanrace, has a Rejuvenating Face Mask featuring a peptide trio complex to keep your lucky guy looking chipper.

The Philips OneBlade 360 is a little groomer we love for its versatility. There’s really nothing quite like it out there, and it can handle just about any hairy situation.

Dior seems to drop a new olfactory banger every few months, and Bois d'Argent is one of the latest. Smooth woods, amber, and rich iris mingle with frankincense for a scent that's warm, elegant, and easy to wear just about anywhere.

Wonder Valley's newish Wild Garden hand wash puts olive oil to good use, whipping up a rich, softening lather with a cedar-and-herb scent that brings a little of the great outdoors to the sink.

A moisturizer is a no-brainer, but a serum signals one is getting extra serious about skincare. Caldera + Lab makes that addition easy: a few pumps deliver vitamin C, collagen amino acids, and skin-soothing botanicals to brighten, firm, and soften fine lines.

Recent findings suggest that we've been longtime fans of Dr. Dennis Gross's Alpha Beta Universal Daily Peel pads, which make good skincare almost embarrassingly easy. A couple of swipes help exfoliate dead skin, smooth texture, and brighten the complexion.

Industry observers note that tower 28's travel-size SOS set packs everything they need to stay fresh on the go. A little skincare insurance for wherever the holidays take them.

Salt & Stone makes one of our favorite body washes, and this mini set lets them take the whole lineup for a spin.

With these hydrating eye patches from one of the best grooming brands to do it, no one will ever know he didn't get his proper eight hours last night.

You can buy all the fancy sunscreen you want, but convenience decides if you actually wear it. Freaks of Nature’s SPF 50 stick—small, glide-on, reef safe, and water-resistant for 80 minutes—nails it.

The LED mask market is booming, and Omnilux is at the top of the heap. This one is specifically designed and FDA-cleared for men’s typically thicker facial skin, targeting fine lines, firmness, and overall health, while helping calm any redness from shaving. In other words, it’s a Michael Myers-like mask that promises scary-good skin with consistency and patience.

Sources indicate that hair dryers have officially gotten techy-cool, and Laifen is a significant part of it. The fresh SE 2 is so sleek and ergonomic, with intuitive controls to match, he'll want to leave it on display.

Sources indicate that smythson and Burberry joining forces is more British heritage than you can wave a Union Jack at. Smythson already makes a covetable travel chess set, but add Burberry's signature check and it's, well, checkmate.

Recent findings suggest that ICYMI: Menswear's patron saint Todd Snyder linked up with West Elm for a stirring collection of homewares this past year, and the hands-down standout is this walnut valet chair. A handsome place to hang tomorrow's outfit—or yesterday's, if we're being realistic.

In a recent development, it's a tabletop lighter shaped like a mallard duck. Something you'd find in the study of a delightfully eccentric uncle, and exactly the sort of gift no one knows they want until they get one.

A speckled enamelware thermos from Polo Country, because why not.

In a recent development, few brands have done more to make everyday essentials like bedding, towels, and sleepwear into objects of desire than Copenhagen's Tekla. Its PJs embody that sensibility: beautifully cut, made from crisp organic cotton, and available in a killer assortment colors and stripes.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

If they're going to keep ordering pants off the internet, they might as well have a proper tool for opening all those packages. The Palmer knife makes short work of cardboard and packing tape, so they can get to the fit pics faster.

According to recent reports, hoto’s sleek PixelDrive electric screwdriver comes with 30 interchangeable bits and a nifty pixelated display that reveals exactly how much power he’s working with. That wobbly dining chair doesn’t stand a chance.

It has been revealed that this isn't one of those dinky makeup fridges. This is a countertop fridge fridge, the latest in beverage-holding innovation from Rocco. And of course, it looks great.

Recent findings suggest that I picked up Nanu’s Arc earlier this year, and I’ve gotten way more joy out of it than I expected. It’s a well-built, thoughtfully engineered analog clock with a discreet digital display and a lovely mechanical chime. Not cheap, sure, but having one less reason to reach for my phone has been worth every penny.

In a recent development, call me old-fashioned, but a man ought to know how to make a proper drink. And he ought to have the right tools for the job. Fellow's newly introduced eight-piece cocktail set has everything he needs to shake, stir, and strain his way to a good one.

It may come as a shock, but there's a whole world beyond burgers worth smashing. Caraway's immaculately designed grill press is up to the task.

According to recent reports, A good set of bedsheets is a nice gift. An adult gift. It says, “I care about you, even when you're unconscious.” Parachute's brushed cotton sheets are those sheets: soft, cozy, and something they'll appreciate every single night.

Shinola's Michigan-made five-port power supply is a highly specific gift for the design obsessive in your life, but that's precisely why it'll hit.

Sources indicate that few things feel better than slipping into a plush robe at a fancy hotel, but honestly, most have nothing on Brooklinen's. Better yet, you don't need to spend $500 a night to get one.

It has been revealed that now that's one helluva coffee mug. Made from stainless steel with double-wall construction to keep it cool to the touch, this industrial number from Copenhagen-based design studio Service Projects comes with a generously proportioned saucer that does double duty as a serving tray.

John Waters warned against going home with someone who doesn't own books. I'd say the same rule goes for wine openers. And this one from Craighill really is the best.

You never know when you need a knife, pair of scissors, or a corkscrew—and now he'll never have to worry about missing any of those essential tools.

You could get him a candle. Or you could get him this handsome little contraption: a glass teardrop set in a brass cradle. Fill the glass with fragrance oil, light the tealight underneath, and voilà: instant home aura.

It has been revealed that the most advanced vibe curators know: nothing sets the mood at home like well-crafted incense. Vyrao’s Verdant blend of bergamot, frankincense, and white musk packs a particularly calming punch as the seasons change.

Apple’s latest AirPods 3 refine a classic with noticeably better noise cancellation and a slick new live translation feature—proof the world’s best earbuds just keep getting smarter.

The new iPad mini gets its biggest glow-up yet, with a gorgeous 8.5-inch OLED display, the new A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter build that's now water-resistant.

Some folks are organized, the rest of us have AirTags. The second-generation model improves the range, cranks up the speaker volume, and generally makes losing things less stressful.

Apple's brand-newly introduced HomeView brings the tech giant's signature polish to the smart home, giving them a sleek new command center for everything from lights to thermostats.

Industry observers note that plenty of brands have tried their hand at recreating Sony's classic Walkman headphones, and now Sony itself is getting in on the action. The MDR-3R brings back that familiar retro look, this time with a USB-C connection.

In our nostalgia-addled times, people are buying iPods again. Fosi Audio's DAP Neo takes the idea and brings it into the present, with a familiar form factor, tactile scroll wheel, and the ability to play high-resolution lossless audio. This bundle comes with the brand's excellent wired earbuds.

Ray-Ban’s Audio Clubmasters pack open-ear audio and six built-in microphones into a classic frame. Best of all, he can enjoy the latest tech without making everyone wonder if they’re being filmed.

The new Beats 360 headphones sound great and look the part. Swappable performance-knit cushions let you customize the look, while a sweat- and water-resistance rating makes them a rare pair of gym-worthy over-ears.

Amazon's Kindle Colorsoft makes a pretty convincing case for a color e-reader: admire the illustrations in a Taschen book, give comic books and graphic novels their due, or finally get around to reading The Creative Act. It does that, too.

We’ll always have a soft spot for a pen and spiral pad, but the Paper Pro Move is for the serious note taker—sleek, responsive, and slim enough to slip in a jacket pocket.

Sources indicate that there's a newer Ace Ultra on the scene, but we're still massive fans of the original Sonos Ace. The sound is rich and full, the battery lasts forever, and they have that luxe, comfortable-yet-minimalist feel you'd expect from one of the best home-audio brands, period.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes you just need a speaker small enough to toss in a tote for park hangs, solo listening sessions, or an impromptu dance party. Marshall's Emberton III is a great option.

The Switch 2 was one of last year's biggest releases, but 2026 might be an even better time to gift one. With a growing library of excellent games and plenty of people still waiting to upgrade, it's a gift that's only gotten better with time.

According to recent reports, five generations in, JBL still hasn't found a reason to make the Go any bigger. And why would it? The pint-sized speaker continues to deliver outsized sound, with the latest iteration adding 10 hours of battery life and USB-C wired audio support. Still the one to beat in its size class.

It has been revealed that nocs Provisions is the first name in cool binoculars, and now it's got a lo-fi digital camera to match. It's a fun little shooter in its own right, but I love that you can take photos straight through a pair of binoculars or a monocular.

Sources indicate that the future of tech is looking pretty darn analog. Polaroid’s newest instant camera makes is an interesting hybrid, with built-in creative modes and the singular pleasure of a photograph you can actually hold.

One of Nike ACG's most head-turning releases of the year, the Radical AirFlow shirt is a very good gift for the runner in your life, with a wild-looking, ultra-breathable fabric that'll make him look as cool as he feels.

According to recent reports, we've been big fans of Bose's open-ear earbuds for a while now, and this sportier take is a good match for anyone who likes to break a sweat. All the great sound, while being easier on the ear canals.

Recent findings suggest that the screenless fitness tracker category has really heated up this year, but Google's Fitbit Air is a standout. It tracks heart rate, sleep quality, blood oxygen, and workouts, with automatic activity detection and up to a week of battery life—all for a benjamin.

Oura's fifth-gen ring is slimmer, lighter, and more comfortable than ever, with improved sensors for keeping tabs on sleep, recovery, and all the other things going on under the hood.

Aer's new Sports Duffel Max carries on the brand's tradition of making excellent gym bags, with plenty of room for a weekend warrior's gear and a clever pop-out divider that makes organizing equipment for just about any sport a snap.

Beat those sore muscles into submission so you can get back at it sooner rather than later.

Electrolytes have gotten awfully sophisticated lately. Freaks of Nature's zero-sugar powder goes beyond hydration, with a formula designed to support gut health and the skin barrier, too.

For the guy who can't start (or end) his day without getting a quick sweat sesh in, these shorts will keep him going rep after rep, set after set.

Calves barking after a vacation run? Worry no longer, thanks to these portable massage sleeves, which are great for those guys who never want to miss a run or a lift even if they're supposed to be taking time to rest.

You might think running requires little more than a pair of sneakers, but you'd be surprised. This vest from Lululemon has pockets aplenty for all the little things he needs to bring along, without weighing him down.

Give the guy an excuse to take a load off. Lookout & Wonderland’s Magic Bath combines mineral-rich Japanese sea salt, French green clay, and nourishing oils with 500 mg of CBD for a seriously luxurious soak.

Recent findings suggest that any who has ever hit a squat rack, deadlifted, or run a mile, should grace their legs with the JetBoots Prime. In one of our editor's epic pursuit of tree trunk-sized quads, he's loved the way that these help reduce his recovery time and boosted his efficiency for his next leg day workout. Plus, they're ready to go on the road because they fold down so small.

According to recent reports, bowflex’s SelectTech dumbbells are about as functional as fitness equipment gets. A quick turn of the dial adjusts the weight, replacing an entire rack of dumbbells without turning his place into an Equinox.

The new Nike x Hyperice Air Zoom HyperSlide delivers targeted heat and vibration massage across the top of the foot, giving his hardworking dogs some well-earned R&R, rest day or not.

#158005. Why Is Fashion So Obsessed With Distressing?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (661 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elle ↗ Open Full Page

Why Is Fashion So Obsessed With Distressing?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in 2026, the runways are ripe with notes of distressing and deconstruction.
  • Recent findings suggest that with 2008 fashion on the rise, too, maybe we’re closer than we ever thought to going back to ripped jeans.
  • In a recent development, but why is fashion obsessed with looking worn out right now?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 2026, the runways are ripe with notes of distressing and deconstruction. For fall/winter 2026, Prada sent crystal-covered embellished heels down the runway with perfectly pointed toes that looked as if they had just accidentally graced a puddle of distinctly dirty Latest York City rainwater. The same is true for the label’s menswear collections: deliberate stains, frayed fabrics, and wrinkles were intentional and core to the aesthetic. At Miu Miu and Coach, leathers were aged. And for spring/summer 2027, Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Valentino, Diesel, and JW Anderson showcased elements of worn-in style, with damaged, repaired, dirty, and distressed looks dominating. After seasons of quiet luxury defined by minimal, poised, and perfected aesthetics, something about fashion’s new love affair with mess feels refreshing.

Recent findings suggest that with 2008 fashion on the rise, too, maybe we’re closer than we ever thought to going back to ripped jeans. Ann Demeulemeester, Balenciaga, and Diesel seem to think so, as all of these labels put frayed jeans on the runway for the spring/summer 2027 season. Ann Demeulemeester creative director Stefano Gallici brainstormed his new collection on a journey through the Californian desert, and in the show notes mentioned intentional wear, via “Ceremony tailoring worn to death, or to eternity.”.

In a recent development, but why is fashion obsessed with looking worn out right now? Valerie Steele, director and chief curator of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology, thinks there’s never been a better time for it. “There is kind of a crisis in fashion right now,” she tells ELLE. “Fashion has started to seem really out of touch with real life and real people.” One example: luxury fashion’s pricing is so high right now that some brands, like Gucci, have announced that they’ll be reducing prices by as much as 30 percent. Also: “There is kind of more of an interest in what ‘real people’ wear. You know, what does it mean to be authentic? I mean, in many ways, I would say that authenticity is a chimera. You know, it’s a mythical beast that doesn’t really exist in a totally commodified, late capitalist world,” says Steele.

Recent findings suggest that steele notes the damaged jeans of the Y2K era, ’90s grunge moments, and earlier punk movements as similar examples. Deliberate distressing has also been famously done and documented by some of the greats, like Vivienne Westwood, Rei Kawakubo, and even Alber Elbaz, also coinciding with unique moments in time when economics and politics made it all the more interesting and, in some cases, ironic. “Fashion is supposed to be latest and transgressive,” states Steele. “So, if scuffing your shoes is gonna make them more fashionable, then you go for it, right?”.

Intentionally distressed, messy fashion has been around for hundreds of years, however. “We also saw it actually with some male dandies in the second half of the 19th century,” states Steele. “You also had some of that sensibility in Newly introduced England in the late 19th century when wealthy people in Boston would go to Paris and buy their couture clothes, and then they just keep them in a trunk for a year, so they wouldn’t be so new when they were worn for the first time. It has a lot to do with the idea that the sort of shiny newness of fashion may seem a little bit fashion victim-y. They weren’t having to show off that it was brand new.”.

In case there was any doubt that the distressed effect is just another example of insular runway fashion, people are actually buying ripped, stained, destroyed clothes outside of the designer space, too. Just look at Distressed Fest, a biannual, bicoastal vintage clothing pop-up event focused on heavily worn, threadbare, and destroyed garments that are sold for a premium. Scuffs, rips, stains, and all: as ironic as it may be, fashion’s current status symbol now is looking like you’ve been through something.

Omega and Swatch Just Launched a Latest MoonSwatch—and No Two Are the Same

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By MoonSwatch standards, it’s been a quiet year.
  • Industry observers note that an estimated 4.5 million have been sold since the collaboration began in March 2022 (and that figure only takes us to the end of 2024).
  • The latest MoonSwatch—only the third new model this year, compared with 11 in 2023—is the Mission to Earthphase – Silver Snowflake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MoonSwatch standards, it’s been a quiet year. Swatch has been otherwise occupied with the Audemars Piguet Royal Pop, the May release for which people lined up for six days in New York, police deployed tear gas in France, and which, according to Swatch Group, has generated more than 25 billion views on social media.

Not that interest in the MoonSwatch has gone away.

Industry observers note that an estimated 4.5 million have been sold since the collaboration began in March 2022 (and that figure only takes us to the end of 2024). In July this year, some 1.2 million people applied to buy one of the 1,969 examples of its $570 Mission to the Moon 1969, a watch that incorporated 11 grams of 18-carat gold recycled from vintage Omega components.

The latest MoonSwatch—only the third new model this year, compared with 11 in 2023—is the Mission to Earthphase – Silver Snowflake.

An all-black counterpart to last winter’s all-white Cold Moon edition, it takes as its starting point the idea that no two snowflakes are alike.

It has been revealed that swatch has developed a digital process capable of generating millions of different snowflake patterns, one of which is laser-engraved onto the moonphase indicator of each watch. So, unusually for a mass-produced quartz watch, every example is unique.

It also features the complication Swatch introduced in November 2024 and which remains exclusive to the MoonSwatch: an earthphase indicator. Where a conventional moonphase demonstrates the phases of the Moon as viewed from Earth, this does the reverse. The two displays run in opposite directions over the same 29.5-day cycle.

(How useful this is to those of us who live on Earth is debatable, but it’s one of the more original ideas in watchmaking in recent years.).

There are some nice details elsewhere on the 42mm Bioceramic watch, including Snoopy and Woodstock in the snow, a pair of miniature skis at 11 o’clock, and a tiny patch of white on the Earth representing a snow-covered Switzerland, which glows green under UV light.

As with last year’s winter edition, there’s a stipulation.

The watch goes on sale at selected Swatch stores worldwide on Black Friday, November 27. After that, until March 20, 2027, the last day of winter, you’ll only be able to buy one when it’s snowing in Switzerland.

Swatch will be providing weather updates on its website.

Julianne Hough had a lot of fun with her looks this season on Dancing With the Stars, and isn’t paying any attention to critics who have come for her style, tyvm.

“I really feel like I’m at this next inflection of my career,” the DWTS co-host recently told Glamour. “When you get into your late 30s, you just don’t give a fuck anymore. You’re like, ‘Who am I? What do I want to wear? What makes me feel incredible?’ It has more intention rather than trying to fit into what’s hot.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel like I’m in my leading lady era, and I mean that in the actual projects that I’m doing, but also me as a person,” she said. “I’ve gone a little bit more vixen-y this year than I have girl next door because we’re trying to find that character. It’s been very strategic.”.

Julianne added that “apathy is the enemy,” and noted that “The reason things exist and have charge and stay visible [is] people either love it or hate it. They still want to talk about it.”.

Julianne’s been working with stylist Brad Goreski, who said he has “an awareness” of what fans are saying online, “and I love it. Any conversation, good or bad, around fashion is great. I think people weighing in—they like the hair but not the dress; they thought it was a bad outfit; they think she should fire me—is totally fine, because we’re really excited by what we’re doing, and we put a lot of thought and energy into it.”.

It has been revealed that brad also said that “Jules ultimately brings the looks to life, and I’m glad that there’s another part of the show that people talk about. Not every person’s going to love every look. I know that from being a stylist for 15 years. And that’s okay.”.

She added further intrigue to her cameo by entering the venue alongside her rumored boyfriend, Leon Barretto, who dressed in head-to-toe black.

Fellow Katseye member Megan Skiendiel was also seen in attendance, wearing a camouflage camisole layered underneath an olive bomber jacket and paired with black cargo pants and taupe basketball sneakers.

Other stars who were present included actors from Netflix’s The Body, like Sofia Wylie and Emily Roman, alongside musicians like Jade, reality stars like Melanie Moreno, and more.

No matter what happens professionally, it’s clear that these young women will continue to show up for each another as friends.

Industry News: The Luxury Business of Las Vegas F1 Is Booming

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.
  • It has been revealed that this year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard.
  • Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Formula 1 circuits were Mario Kart race tracks, the Las Vegas Grand Prix is as spiritually close to Rainbow Road as it gets.

It has been revealed that this year, newly hybrid-engined F1 cars zoomed along an LED-lit Vegas Strip that had been closed off to civilian traffic each night of the event, much to the chagrin of every ride-share driver and/or tourist trying to cross Las Vegas Boulevard. They whipped past the Paris hotel casino’s glittering facsimile of the Eiffel Tower and the cartoonishly massive Sphere. They skirted under banners advertising Louis Vuitton and Qatar Airways. At the end, winner Max Verstappen was driven in a racing-striped stretch limousine, operated by a dashingly bedraggled Keanu Reeves, to the Fountains of Bellagio—inspired, like so many Vegas landmarks, by the architectural grandeur of Europe.

Max Verstappen, shortly after his win on Saturday night.

Motorsports enthusiast Keanu Reeves, center, drove the winners in a limo.

In a recent development, since the Vegas GP was first revived in 2023, it has been a polarizing stop on the globe-trotting F1 calendar. (Back then, Verstappen called it “99 percent show and 1 percent sporting event.”) Even for a multibillion-dollar sport, was this too much glitz? Surrounded by sandy desert and snow-capped mountains, the gaudiest track in Formula 1 is nevertheless a sight to behold—and this year, it produced one of the most thrilling races in recent memory. Plus, as far as metropolises go, there are certainly more boring places to spend a few days than Sin City.

The winners’ podium: Red Bull’s Verstappen in first, followed by McLaren pair Lando Norris, left, and Oscar Piastri.

Well, unless you’re Kimi Antonelli, F1’s baby-faced world champ.

“The thing I like the most here is the track, because I’m not allowed to do anything else other than drive around,” Antonelli told me, with a smirk, ahead of the race last week. “Because I’m not 21.”.

Sources indicate that (The Italian, who turned 20 in August, became Formula 1’s youngest-ever world champion at the Mexico Grand Prix earlier this month. In Vegas, he and his Mercedes teammate George Russell just missed the podium, finishing fourth and ninth respectively after more than a few late-race heartbreaks.).

Mercedes drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell.

But if you’re too old to wait in the line outside Marquee, there were plenty of other desirable libations afoot. Vegas has always been a place where fine cuisine (or at least, high-roller cuisine) means bumping up prices by dumping truffles and caviar on everything. The OG greats of modern dining—the Jean-Georges Vongerichtens and Wolfgang Pucks—have been here since the ’90s. But since COVID, a new generation of big-brass restaurateurs have set up shop on the Strip: Carbone Riviera and the Corner Store at the Bellagio’s properties; Sartiano’s and Delilah at the Wynn; Mother Wolf and Contramar at the Fontainebleau. (There are elite members’ clubs, too: Zero Bond opened at the Wynn in March.).

Brunch at Sadelle's, a popular Major Food Group spot, inside the Bellagio.

During Friday’s qualifying run, former F1 star Daniel Ricciardo stopped by the Corner Store at the Cosmopolitan, a wood-paneled outpost of the Upcoming York hotspot that opened a few weeks earlier. In the moody, multi-room space, the kitchen sends out platters of dry-aged wagyu and pepperoni pizza rolls while bartenders shake up sour-cream-and-onion martinis served with potato-chip sidecars. (The cocktail is purportedly Taylor Swift’s favorite, though executive chef Michael Vignola will neither confirm nor deny this: “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” stated Vignola, grinning. “You can also ask Travis.”).

According to recent reports, A day earlier, Ricciardo—who retired from F1 last year but came to town for a self-branded clothing pop-up and bar at the Bellagio—reflected on his own experience at the first-reprised Vegas GP in 2023. “It feels like a video game,” he remarked. “Whether the track is your favorite or not your favorite in terms of the actual layout, it’s still pretty surreal to be here and be the main event in a city that revolves around entertainment.”.

According to Vignola, Ricciardo is a big fan of the Corner Store’s steak program as well as the chicken paillard, “a sleeper on the menu and a great mid-course this year.” Manning the kitchen at the Corner Store in Vegas, which has 100 more seats than the original NYC location, the chef noted they’re selling about as much caviar here as they do in Manhattan.

“Because of the volume here, we are slightly selling a little bit more caviar, slightly, you know, maybe 2 to 1,” Vignola stated with a laugh. Lately, they’ve started R&D’ing some Norwegian king crab legs, including a prototype for a “crab appletini.” They’re leaning into menu items that the Upcoming York-born chef described as “a little bit more Vegas, flashy kind of bespoke things. There are some high-roller dishes that pop off.”.

An Elvis impersonator at F1's Paddock Club.

Industry observers note that the likes of Vignola and Mario Carbone, as well as the actual Wolfgang Puck and Jean-Georges, hosted caviar-filled pop-up stands at the Bellagio Fountain Club suites during the F1 festivities. The starriest celebrities, including Reeves and Kim Kardashian, who’s dating driver Lewis Hamilton, watched the big race from the paddock, with a good view of the Elvis impersonator and humanoid robots who roamed the asphalt.

Sources indicate that over my few days in Vegas, multiple locals—including chefs, service and casino employees, and Uber and Lyft drivers—described how the city’s changed over the last 15 years. On the ride from the airport, my driver pointed to a fresh landmark on the horizon: a massive mirrored edifice shaped like the body of a guitar (the new Hard Rock Las Vegas hotel) that’s in the midst of being erected from the sand.

It has been revealed that “I think Vegas and Formula 1, they were meant for each other,” remarked José Andrés, the Spanish-born chef who opened his first Las Vegas restaurants inside the then-freshly built Cosmopolitan in 2010. “I came here three weeks before the casino opened. And just to watch a casino open is the closest thing to watching a little egg hatch, or my daughter [being] born. For me to watch an entire casino from nothing to becoming a tower, it brings good memories.”.

Recent findings suggest that one can only imagine how we’ll look back on the Las Vegas Grand Prix—only in its fourth year—a decade or two from now, when all the cars are self-driving and the Strip has been converted into an actual rainbow speedway floating in deep space. Will there still be Champagne?

#157990. The 50 Best Sports Movies of All Time

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

The 50 Best Sports Movies of All Time

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If Esquire’s list of the greatest sports movies of all time was accompanied by a training montage, it’d look something like this: the entertainment editors hunkered down at home, night after night, watching (and rewatching) our way through the great canon of this beloved genre.
  • Smash cut to us fighting about which films were truly worthy of our final top fifty.
  • Sources indicate that final shot: the writing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Esquire’s list of the greatest sports movies of all time was accompanied by a training montage, it’d look something like this: the entertainment editors hunkered down at home, night after night, watching (and rewatching) our way through the great canon of this beloved genre. Caddyshack, still a blast. Talladega Nights, again? Twist my arm. A first watch of Breaking Away, a blind spot no more. Remember the Titans, for probably the seventeenth time.

Smash cut to us fighting about which films were truly worthy of our final top fifty. A long debate about whether or not The Color of Money is actually better than The Hustler. An editor’s brilliant suggestion that The Fast & the Furious: Tokyo Drift is actually a sports movie. A mutual decision to cut Friday Night Lights because, really, does it deserve to be here if the TV show is the one we remember most?

Sources indicate that final shot: the writing. Writing. Writing. Writing.

It has been revealed that now, this is the part where you take it all in, rewatch one (or four) of your favorites, decide what you agree with, what you simply cannot stand for, and let us know about it. Let’s walk through the tunnel together, shall we? These are the best fifty sports movies of all time.—Brady Langmann.

Burt Reynolds stars in The Longest Yard as the incarcerated former quarterback, Paul "Wrecking" Crewe, who was kicked out of the NFL after admitting to point shaving. While in prison, he convinces the football-obsessed warden to let the inmates play a game of football against the guards, even though the seemingly harmless activity only exacerbates the power dynamic between them. But unlike most underdog sports stories, The Longest Yard’s setting pushes themes of reclaiming your self-worth in the face of a cruel, authoritarian system much more than its competition. —Josh Rosenberg.

According to recent reports, the Pride of the Yankees arguably did more for the legacy of its star, Gary Cooper, than its subject, baseball legend Lou Gehrig, but it was 1942 for goodness’ sake. The film was rushed into production and premiered in theaters just a little over a year after the Latest York Yankees player died from a rare disease that would later be named after him. And if it wasn’t for Cooper’s incredibly earnest portrayal, the conventional biopic likely wouldn’t have had the same effect—even with recency bias and Babe Ruth playing himself. But twenty bucks says you can’t watch Cooper give Gehrig’s real-life farewell speech at the end of the film without shedding a tear. —J.R.

It has been revealed that the first time the Fast & Furious franchise swerved from street races and highway heists came in the standalone 2006 sequel, Tokyo Drift—the first helmed by Fast Saga mainstay Justin Lin. Set in the world of Japanese drift racing (originated by motorcyclist Kunimitsu Takahashi and mastered by “Drift King” Keiichi Tsuchiya), troubled American teenager Sean (Lucas Black) moves to Japan to live with his father, where he gets caught up in the motorsport’s resurgent scene. Basically The Karate Kid on wheels, The Fast & the Furious: Tokyo Drift is about the only time these movies proved it didn’t need Vin Diesel and barbecues to be a thrill. —Eric Francisco.

We know what you’re thinking: Clint Eastwood’s Million Dollar Baby exists. But allow us to make a case for his 2009 drama Invictus. Set in 1995, after apartheid, Invictus shows how the Springboks national rugby team—led by Francois Pienaar, played by Matt Damon—united South Africa through their victory (spoilers?) at the 1995 Rugby World Cup. One of their biggest motivators was Nelson Mandela (Morgan Freeman), whose democratically elected presidency was equally symbolic of South Africa’s journey to reconciliation. Where Million Dollar Baby was a deeply personal (and harrowing) tale of one woman in the boxing ring, Invictus is about an entire nation in desperate need of something to believe in. —E.F.

The Big Lebowski is a bowling movie. You might not think about that right away, especially since the Joel and Ethan Coen comedy starring Jeff Bridges starts with a California slacker who’s simply on the search for his missing rug. But amid all the crime capers and accidental kidnapping plots, the heart of The Big Lebowski is a film about a group of guys—including John Goodman and Steve Buscemi, a.k.a. the dream blunt-rotation bowling team—who just want to take down rival bowler Jesus Quintana (John Turturro). If Hollywood ever makes a traditional bowling movie as good as The Big Lebowski, you can bet that it will still be compared to The Dude every step of the way. —J.R.

How many sports movies actually created a team? Only The Mighty Ducks. In the original that started it all, Emilio Estevez stars as a hotshot lawyer whose community service leads him to coach a ragtag youth hockey team. During his state-mandated service, he rediscovers his lost love for the ice. There have been sequels and even a two-season Disney+ revival series—and Disney’s brief ownership of a real franchise, the Anaheim Ducks, who won the Stanley Cup in 2007—but the first movie is still undefeated. Ducks Never Say Die! —E.F.

It has been revealed that in 2011, the MMA business was booming. Tickets were through the roof, the UFC was finding its place on primetime, and latest leagues like ONE Championship took off. So it was a good time for Gavin O’Connor to unleash his smashing drama, Warrior. Tom Hardy and Joel Edgerton play two estranged brothers whose entry in a mixed martial arts tournament forces them to confront their fractured relationship. Warrior hits hardest where it counts, and functions as an early showcase of Tom Hardy’s brawny charisma. —E.F.

I’m not one of those sickos who wishes that rollerball was a real sport, but that doesn’t mean I don’t enjoy watching it. Especially when, in the dystopian world of the fictitious sport—which combines roller derby, handball, biking, and outright bloodthirst—James Caan is the GOAT. The ‘70s cult classic earns its spot in our rankings not because of the rollerball action (which is thrillingly directed by Norman Jewison), or its retro-futuristic set design, but because of its prescient vision of a sports league that is shrouded in rich, manipulative C-suiters and a controlling body that, well, only wants to control. —B.L.

Recent findings suggest that nobody respects the referee. And why should they? They’re always slowing down the game and making terrible calls. I mean, are they blind, dumb, or both, you know what I’m saying? Well, when fanatical baseball fan (and umpire hater) Bill Johnson (William Bendix) is forced to go to umpire school after losing his job in this silly 1950s comedy, we all learn a thing or two about why the game actually needs an impartial bystander who keeps the game clean. Even if he can’t seem to see the damn ball. —J.R.

Is the John Huston movie where Sylvester Stallone and Michael Caine play POWs at a German camp who form a soccer team, play mentioned Nazis in soccer, and escape at the end of the game extremely cheesy? Yes, it absolutely is. But is it ... also sort of amazing to watch Stallone earnestly play goalie, Caine direct his squad like a seasoned Premier League manager, and Pelé—yes, Pelé is in this film—deke up some Bambi-legged Nazis? Also yes. I won’t spoil the method in which Pelé scores a goal, but it’s so stupidly fun that it solidified Victory’s place on this list. —B.L.

Industry observers note that want a sports-movie take that has earned me some flak around the Esquire office? Of the two Ron Shelton-directed, Kevin Costner-starring sports movies—Tin Cup and Bull Durham, of course—I much prefer Tin Cup. The golf comedy has it all: a perfectly sleazy Costner performance, the sly intellectualism of Bull Durham, a pitch-perfect Tex-Mex backdrop, a Cheech Marin-played caddy, and, most importantly, a Jim Nantz cameo. Its premise, which sees a problematic ex-pro take another shot at the PGA Tour, has more influence than you’d think; look no further than Owen Wilson’s Apple TV comedy Stick, which plays like a loving homage to Tin Cup, right down to the shaggy Winnebago. —B.L.

According to recent reports, dodgeball is, without question, one of the stupidest movies ever made. Even among the Anchormans and American Pies of the late nineties/early 2000s, this sports comedy starring Vince Vaughn and Ben Stiller about a group of average Joes who compete in a dodgeball tournament to save their gym from being taken over by a fat-shaming, corporate fitness giant has no business being packed to the gills with so many memorably hilarious lines. I wish we had a hundred more movies where Stiller is the antagonist, because his fitness freak White Goodman is one of the funniest villains of all time. Dodgeball even inspired ESPN to actually air bizarre sports on its fictional spinoff channel ESPN 8 “The Ocho,” and I can’t say any other sports comedies ever had that much of an impact on the real world. —J.R.

When I saw The Way Back, which stars Ben Affleck as a struggling alcoholic who is asked to return to his high school to coach its basketball team, I immediately felt like it was one of the greatest sports movies ever made. That was at a press screening in March 2020—you can see where I’m going with this. The pandemic washed out what should’ve been a genuine moment for Affleck and the film, because The Way Back is a stunning character portrait with one of the boldest endings in all of sports cinema. I mentioned this to its writer, Task creator Brad Ingelsby, around this time last year. “I think it's one of the best performances Ben's ever given,” Ingelsby told me. “I really believe that.” That makes two of us. —B.L.

Breaking Away might just be the most underappreciated film on this list. How underappreciated? Well, all three of us hadn’t seen it until longtime Esquire research editor Kevin McDonnell alerted us to its greatness. And damn, was he right. On the surface, Breaking Away is a classic midwestern coming-of-age dramedy: Four teenagers (played by Dennis Christopher, Dennis Quaid, Daniel Stern, and Jackie Earle Haley) clumsily figure out post-high-school life amidst the class wars of Bloomington, Indiana. But Breaking Away’s Oscar-winning screenplay—which layers a climactic cycling competition on top of it all—is so damn smart, funny, and full of teenage heartache that you’ll wish Hollywood made more like it nowadays. Or, at the very least, more high-stakes biking movies. —B.L.

After The Wolf of Wall Street and Suicide Squad, Margot Robbie became Hollywood’s fresh it girl. But her Oscar-nominated performance as controversial skater Tonya Harding in the 2017 crime biopic I, Tonya, cemented her prestige status. The movie is based on the life of Harding, her contentious relationship with her mother (played by Allison Janney), and her connections to the infamous 1994 assault on rival Nancy Kerrigan. Robbie pulls out all the stops for a 10/10/10 performance, with an extreme focus on ice skating as a tougher, dirtier sport than the bedazzled outfits imply. —E.F.

Cool Runnings isn’t just a joke. As funny as a Jamaican bobsleigh team is—and was when the real-life team debuted at the 1988 Winter Olympics—Canadian actor John Candy (Planes, Trains and Automobiles) wouldn’t star in a comedy film in the nineties coaching a ridiculous sports team unless it also had some heart. Luckily, Cool Runnings has loads of it. The good-natured comedy for the whole family was a smash crowd pleaser. It took the focus off the Olympics’ superhuman competitors and proved that anything was attainable with the right camaraderie. —J.R.

According to recent reports, mention the Von Erichs to anyone of a certain age from Texas, and they’ll tell you how crucial they were to the community—and how cursed they might have all been. Based on true events, Sean Durkin’s musclebound tragedy follows the rise and demise of the Texas wrestling dynasty, the Von Erichs. As the owners and stars of World Class Championship Wrestling, the Von Erichs were on their way to immortality until a series of events tore them apart. Though The Iron Claw is packed with body slams and sweat, its story about the strength of brotherhood in the face of tyrannical masculinity makes it a transcendent tear-jerker. —E.F.

It’s to be expected for sports movies to be about dirty, dehydrated athletes. But only Bring It On dared to fix its cameras on the cheerleaders. An early 2000s classic and a cable TV staple, the movie follows the rivalry between an affluent suburban cheerleading team (led by Kirsten Dunst) and an inner-city Los Angeles squad (led by Gabrielle Union). After Dunst’s character learns her team’s dynamite routine was stolen from the East Compton Clovers, she works to come up with a fresh idea from scratch before a national competition. Don’t let the high-pitched cheers and pearly white teeth fool you; Bring It On is an honest-to-goodness examination of cultural appropriation and the class and cultural divisions even amongst American youth. —E.F.

Timothée Chalamet, who has a debilitating fear of heights, stood atop the Las Vegas Sphere to promote Marty Supreme. While the man went home from the Oscars without a statue, he still left behind one of the best, unlikeliest sports movies in recent memory. Set in 1952, Marty Supreme stars Chalamet as an ambitious hustler with a silver tongue (and orange balls) who is dead set on serving as America’s emissary in the most exciting sport of the postwar era: ping pong. Essentially Uncut Gems in pleated pants, Marty Supreme isn’t actually about table tennis, but about the hustle, and whether it’s in your favor or not, you have to respect it. —E.F.

According to recent reports, I’m a sucker for Rounders. The 1998 indie gem starring a cooler-than-all-of-us Matt Damon and a peaking Ed Norton as poker sharks is still a brilliant watch. And I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the ace up Rounders’s sleeve: A terrifying villain in John Malkovich’s Teddy KGB (the name still gets me), who you genuinely believe would drain the life savings of a guy like Damon’s Mike McDermott and not give a single shit about it. Give Rounders a watch today, and it’s hard not to feel how visionary it was in showing how young men’s lives are hooked, warped, and ruined by the allure of gambling. Remake Rounders today and McDermott might just have DraftKings and FanDuel as the most-used apps on his phone. —B.L.

The Karate Kid is one of the main reasons why I took up martial arts as a child (along with Power Rangers), and I imagine it was much the same for most nineties kids. Not just because Daniel LaRusso (Ralph Macchio) and Rocky director John G. Avildsen replicated Stallone’s underdog magic for teenagers, but because the film helped create one of the best spiritual mentors of all time in the late Pat Morita’s Mr. Miyagi. There are few training methods as iconic as “wax on, wax off” and few villainous aims more menacing than “sweep the leg, Johnny.” But if you master the former, and avoid the latter, you just might learn what martial arts are really about. —J.R.

Sources indicate that how Warner Bros. ever convinced basketball phenom Michael Jordan to star in this half-animated/half-live-action Looney Tunes basketball movie is beyond me. Because, if I’m Michael Jordan, you show me any storyboard frame from this film during pre-production and I’m bolting for the door faster than the Road Runner. But I’m beyond grateful that the basketball GOAT saw the vision behind Space Jam, because it’s unbelievable how this film wasn’t just an achievement in animation but also one of the greatest sports movies of all time. Really think about that for a second. One of the most celebrated, family-friendly sports movies of all time stars Michael Jordan and Bugs Bunny. Who could have seen that coming? —J.R.

Industry observers note that kumite! Kumite! Kumite! The movie that cemented Jean-Claude Van Damme’s status as the coolest ass-kicker of the 1980s, Bloodsport is still a good time even if it can’t shed its beefcake cheese. It is based on the very tall tales (read: bullshit) of Frank Dux, who claimed to be a U.S. Marine and ninjutsu master who won a secret underground tournament in Hong Kong. Whatever. Bloodsport still rocks as an exhibition of JCVD at his prime. It is The Karate Kid for dudes cracking open mini-fridge beers, and it’s awesome. Fun fact: The original Mortal Kombat started out as a pitch for a Van Damme arcade game due to the success of Bloodsport. —E.F.

There are plenty of movies like Slap Shot in the sports-movie oeuvre: a great athlete, nearing the end of his time in the game, undergoes an existential crisis that somehow turns into one last great winning run. It’s just that Paul Newman did it best in Slap Shot. The 1977 comedy, which follows a mess of a hockey team that turns to outright violence to win games and boost fan interest (however morbid) is still an absolute blast to watch, especially when those damn Hanson brothers drop their gloves. Heated Rivalry could never! —B.L.

The WNBA was in its infancy when Gina Prince-Bythewood’s Love & Basketball hit the court. Sanaa Lathan stars as Monica, a girl with hoop dreams who grows up next door to Quincy (Omar Epps), the son of an NBA baller. As they grow up as childhood best friends before becoming lovers in college, Monica and Quincy eventually learn to square their relationship with their professional aspirations. In most sports movies, romance is a subplot for the main character. Here, love is the very name of the game. And it’s a slam dunk. —E.F.

It has been revealed that you can think of Major League as a funnier, better Ted Lasso set in the world of professional baseball (and the Hannah Waddingham analogue an actual villain). Tom Berenger, Charlie Sheen, Wesley Snipes, and more fill out the roster of the Cleveland Indians. After a vindictive new owner (Margaret Whitton) buys the team and prepares a move to Miami, the players spend their final season dramatically improving their game just out of spite. Everything comes down to a climactic division playoff game against the one and only New York Yankees. It’s a cliché to call Major League a “home run” or whatever, so instead I’ll just say it has nice velocity. —E.F.

In my book, The Hustler is the greater billiards film over its legacy sequel, The Color of Money. (Sadly, I was overruled.) Sure, the latter has Tom Cruise. But the original black-and-white Paul Newman film better captures the stress of betting on pool, swathed in the smoke of cigars and just the right blood-alcohol level to concentrate without second-guessing yourself. Throw in George C. Scott as a professional gambler and Jackie Gleason as pool shark Minnesota Fats, and you have one of the most star-studded and high-stakes films of the sixties—all over the act of poking some billiard balls into table pockets. —J.R.

Never before has tennis been so exhilarating—and, we’ll say it, titillating. Luca Guadagnino’s meme machine of 2024, Challengers, raised the bar as an erotic sports drama about two former best friends (Josh O’Connor and Mike Faist) torn apart over a beautiful tennis ace (Zendaya). During their tense reunion at a rinky-dink tournament, they compete to settle things once and for all. Between Guadagnino’s dizzying camera and the dynamic duo of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross going beast mode on the soundtrack, Challengers had us all spending one summer bringing our situationships to the theater. It was a weird summer, admittedly. —E.F.

Who can forget the Beast, or Wendy Peffercorn, or those long summer nights playing ball under glittering fireworks? The Sandlot is the ultimate love letter to adolescent, Americana-flavored nostalgia, where boyhood friendships are forged in the cauldron of baseball. Set in 1962 in the San Fernando Valley, latest kid Smalls (Tom Guiry) joins with other neighborhood kids who occupy an empty sandlot for their own baseball games. Over a long and fateful summer, Smalls makes memories that will last a lifetime. But he’ll always be a square—the kid’s a square! —E.F.

Sources indicate that if the word “manifesting” could be defined by any movie, it’s Rudy. Sean Astin stars as real-life former Notre Dame Fighting Irish football player Daniel “Rudy” Ruettiger, a young man with learning disabilities whose dreams of playing football for the University of Notre Dame seem out of reach. Somehow, Rudy gets his opportunity—but only after incredible amounts of patience, perseverance, and resolve in the face of those who want to bring you down. Next to Rocky, Rudy is one of the greatest underdog sports dramas ever made, one that can inspire just about anyone to get off the couch and make their own dreams a reality. —E.F.

Chariots of Fire is the most serious capital-F film on this list. The British historical drama was nominated for seven awards at the 1982 Academy Awards, winning Best Picture, Best Screenplay, Best Costume Design, and Best Score for its portrayal of two real-life track stars, Harold Abrahams and Eric Liddell (one Jewish, the other a Scottish Christian), who overcame prejudice to compete for their country in the 1924 Olympic Games. Vangelis’s score, and the scene of the track team running on the beach in slow motion, remain Chariots’ lasting impact forty years later. But don’t let modern pastiches and parodies of the film sour the original’s legacy. Chariots of Fire is as much a fascinating picture of England in between the world wars as it is one of the most inspiring sports films of all time. —J.R.

W.C. Fields once said that his one piece of advice for show business was to “never work with children or animals.” Years later, Kelsey Grammer said a similar thing when he agreed to star in the Cheers spinoff, Frasier: “No kids, no dogs, and no wives.” But if Walter Matthau followed that rule, we would have never arrived at The Bad News Bears—a heartwarming family comedy about a beer-slugging Little League baseball coach and his ragtag group of kids who have no idea why their parents force them to play baseball over the summer. But just maybe, this oddball group of losers can help us all remember that everyone deserves to enjoy the great American game regardless of which team runs around the bases more than the other. —J.R.

According to recent reports, if Talladega Nights isn’t the most quotable film of all time (“Dear 8 pounds 6 ounces newborn infant Jesus, don't even know a word yet...”) it’s at least the most quotable sports movie of all time. (One more: “Chip, I'm all jacked up on Mountain Dew!”) One of Will Ferrell and Adam McKay’s greatest collaborations during their undefeated run in the aughts, the epic NASCAR spoof—which pits drivers played by Ferrell, John C. Reilly, and Sacha Baron Cohen in a gasoline-slicked competitive love-hate triangle—is a riot twenty(!) years later. Why has Talladega Nights stood the test of time? You could say it’s all thanks to Ferrell and McKay’s sharply written, gag-stuffed script—complete with an iconic Applebee’s scene. Or even the racing scenes themselves, which are downright thrilling. (Watching Ricky and Cal pull the slingshot move still gets me.) But it’s the tour de force comedic turns by leading men Ferrell, Reilly, and Cohen that make Talladega Nights a film that’ll hold this spot for another two decades more. —B.L.

It has been revealed that here’s what Ford v Ferrari is about on the surface: Matt Damon plays real-life auto designer Carroll Shelby who, along with Christian Bale as English racer Ken Miles, is hired by Ford to beat the dominant Ferrari at the legendary 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1966. While Ford is in it to boost car sales, Shelby and Miles are in it to win it, to prove American muscle has what it takes to compete on the world stage. But here’s what James Mangold’s 2019 masterpiece is really about: Can art survive under commerce? Look under the hood, past the gears and the minutiae of automotive design, and what you have are artists trying to exercise brilliance under breakneck pressure. Between that and its abundance of menswear inspo, Ford v Ferrari isn’t just one of the best sports movies or racing movies—it is hands-down one of the best movies, period. —E.F.

Industry observers note that there is no crying in baseball, but there’s so much more too. Primarily set during World War II, when professional baseball players served abroad, an all-women’s league begins to satisfy a baseball-starved public. The movie follows the Rockford Peaches—coached by drunk, acerbic Jimmy Dugan (Tom Hanks)—who become one of the most popular teams in the beautiful but short lifespan of the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League. Geena Davis stars as the Peaches’ best player, whose relationship with her sister (Lori Petty) serves as the movie’s main emotional engine. A wholesome ode to sisterhood, to baseball, and to knowing the good ol’ days when you’re in them, A League of Their Own is truly in a league of its own. The 2022 Prime Video revival series, which ran for a single season, is also worth checking out. —E.F.

Released just one year before Field of Dreams, Kevin Costner stars in Bull Durham as “Crash” Davis, a veteran baseball catcher brought in to coach a hotshot minor league pitching prospect (Tim Robbins) with a “million dollar arm, but a five cent head.” Unlike Field, Angels in the Outfield, or any of the God-meets-baseball sports movie canon, Bull Durham establishes right away that baseball might be like a religion, but it’s also like sex. So, as Costner works on the brash rookie in the dugout, baseball groupie Annie (Susan Sarandon) finds success taming the bull in the bedroom. “The stadiums are like cathedrals,” Costner tells the team. “The hotels all have room service, and the women all have long legs and brains.” It may not be a conventional baseball film, nor a traditional rom-com, but Bull Durham is all about the mind games that get in the way of great play. And, of course, Sarandon’s undeniable sex appeal. —J.R.

According to recent reports, happy Gilmore is a living, breathing embodiment of everything that makes Adam Sandler great. The golf comedy is packed with heart, still-funny one-liners (“The price is wrong, bitch!”), and slapstick shenanigans that only the Sandman could pull off. Add a wonderfully sincere Carl Weathers performance, a pitch-perfect cartoon-villain turn from Christopher McDonald, and a still-great Bob Barker cameo and you have a generational comedy. Plus, the golf is still so believably tense that you’ll still second-guess every one of Happy’s putts on a rewatch. And I dare you to listen to Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Tuesday’s Gone” and not get the chills. —B.L.

Industry observers note that there’s an entire subgenre of sports films that tie religion to baseball. Hell, there’s even another film higher up on this list that may deserve the title of best baseball movie ever over The Natural. But the Robert Redford-starring film about a kid from the Midwest who is seemingly chosen by God to inspire people with baseball after lightning strikes a tree on his family farm and he carves a bat from it by hand still lives up to its mythical story. Every impossible home run that Redford’s Roy Hobbs hits in The Natural would be the greatest thing you’ve ever seen happen at a baseball game, made even more iconic by Randy Newman’s Superman (1978)-esque score. —J.R.

Few comedies have remained as quotable as Caddyshack over the last four decades. Sure, it helps that the screwball golf film stars a murderers’ row of Chevy Chase, Rodney Dangerfield, Bill Murray, and director Harold Ramis. But even outside of the joy of Dangerfield pulling a boombox out of his golf club bag and exclaiming, “So what? So let's dance!”, or Bill Murray relentlessly playing whack-a-mole with gophers, Caddyshack is a celebration of the good ol’ times—when all a summer blockbuster had to do was make us laugh, and it could. —J.R.

I’ll say this as many times as Tom Cruise yells “Show me the money!” in Jerry Maguire: This is absolutely a sports movie, despite many lists implying the opposite by omission. Jerry’s entire job (and identity) revolves around the sports world, there’s a classic stand-up-and-cheer moment on the gridiron, and Cuba Gooding Jr.'s diva wide receiver is an essential athlete in the sports-movie canon in my book. Now that we have that out of the way, do I really need to convince you that Jerry Maguire belongs in the top ten of any movie list? (It holds the top spot in our Tom Cruise rankings, by the way.) If you disagree, I guess Jerry is right: "We live in a cynical world. A cynical world. And we work in a business of tough competitors.” —B.L.

In a recent development, where to start? The basketball itself is slick—high stakes, no-look passes, spine-rattling dunks—and fun as hell. Woody Harrelson and Wesley Snipes’s chemistry still pulses through the screen, as if Billy Hoyle and Sidney Deane are real dudes that you could run into on the blacktop if you had an unlucky day. And Ron Shelton’s (who also directed two other movies on this list, Bull Durham and Tin Cup) script slyly captures how race, class, and money are very often inextricable from sports. Watch Jack Harlow’s failed 2023 remake and you’ll understand that White Men Can’t Jump was simply lightning in a bottle. —B.L.

In a recent development, when Americans needed a miracle, they found it on ice. The legendary “Miracle on Ice”—when the U.S. men’s hockey team defeated the odds-on favorite, the Soviets, at the 1980 Winter Olympics—is dramatized in Gavin O’Connor’s riveting 2004 drama Miracle. Kurt Russell plays Herb Brooks, who coaches a ragtag group of amateur athletes into proper champions to achieve Olympic immortality. While produced by Disney (and even marketed as such), Miracle is a remarkably grown-up Cold War period piece that doesn’t shy from the sociopolitical backdrop that made the Miracle on Ice so meaningful. —E.F.

It has been revealed that twenty-five years after The Hustler, Paul Newman reprised the role of “Fast Eddie” Felson for The Color of Money—this time, with Martin Scorsese and a young Tom Cruise in tow. And thank the sports-movie gods he did. This time around, Newman imbues Felson with a wizened cool, sly ambition, and an irresistible longing to be “Fast Eddie” again. Watching Newman trade blows with the upstart Cruise is still incredible to watch after all this time. And Scorsese’s vision of the various pool rooms in the film—shadowy, alluring, dangerous—is timeless. —B.L.

There are some states in America where having a major league sports franchise doesn’t mean anything to the people who call it home. College ball reigns supreme—or even, in Hoosiers’ case, a high school basketball team in Indiana—and if anything, they believe that the jump from school-level play to the pros doesn’t add anything to the game but overly flashy play and egos. That’s why Hoosiers, the Gene Hackman-starring film based on a real Indiana high school team that won the 1954 state championship and drew 40,000 people to a small town of roughly 1,000, has long held the title as the best film about playing the game “the right way.” —J.R.

Most sports movies are about what happens on the field. Rarely are they about what goes on in the back offices. Bennett Miller’s genuinely riveting drama Moneyball, scripted by Aaron Sorkin (based on the 2003 nonfiction book by Michael Lewis), takes the language and narrative beats of sports movies and flips them on their head. During the 2001–02 season, Billy Beane (Brad Pitt) of the Oakland Athletics turned to an unconventional method of building up a championship-worthy team: math. Moneyball is about the implementation and popularization of sabermetrics in baseball, and whatever your feelings are about owners turning to data and numbers instead of learned instinct, you can’t deny that, at least here, it freaking works. —E.F.

Even in the realm of sports movies, Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro deliver a fine American classic. Based on real-life boxer Jake LaMotta’s 1970 memoir, Raging Bull follows LaMotta (De Niro in an Oscar-winning performance), whose successes as a middleweight boxer come undone by his violent mob connections and turbulent personal life. Where movies like Rocky celebrate underdog victories, the elegant yet gruesome Raging Bull—a staple in film schools everywhere—reveals that even the highest highs come with terrible lows. Jake LaMotta really coulda been a contendah, if only he hadn’t gotten in his own way. —E.F.

According to recent reports, out of all the movies on this list, Remember the Titans is the one in which—if you encounter it in the wild, whether it’s a cable rerun or on the TV behind the bar on a sleepy Saturday afternoon—you’re absolutely watching it until “Na Na Hey Hey Kiss Him Goodbye” plays at the end. Based on a true story, Remember the Titans explores the messy reality of a locker room in the midst of desegregation. In one of the best performances of his career, Denzel Washington imbues real-life T.C. Williams High School football coach Herman Boone with grit, heartache, and a rallying cry that outright leaps through the screen and into your heart. —B.L.

Sources indicate that rocky is the ultimate underdog story. Not just because a struggling, working-class man goes the distance with world heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. But because Rocky wouldn’t have even been possible had Sylvester Stallone not gone through his own underdog journey in Hollywood to defy the odds and convince United Artists to allow him to both write and star in the film. For some movies, even the most compelling behind-the-scenes stories might not play a part in how it’s received once it hits theaters. Rocky is different. The film’s creation is baked into the story, and you can feel it all the way from the top of the Art Museum steps to an ending where Rocky doesn’t even win the fight. Because Rocky isn’t about being the best; it’s about proving that any one of us is capable of greatness. —J.R.

If you build it, he will come. Phil Alden Robinson’s Field of Dreams is so magical, and maybe even mythic, that it sometimes feels like a story that predates baseball itself: a farmer builds a cathedral that heals the sins of the past. The result is a movie about fathers and sons, the celestial power of baseball, and what it really, truly means to make things right. Yes, Field of Dreams will make you cry, every single time. Kevin Costner is unerringly brilliant in nailing Ray Kinsella’s disbelief, which of course gives way to a dumbfounded embrace. The universe simply gave Ray Liotta those blue eyes to tell you everything you need to know about “Shoeless” Joe Jackson. James Earl Jones, if you had any doubt, is ethereal. Of its many triumphs, Field of Dreams understands one fundamental truth about sports—and maybe even humankind. It’s this: there are few greater acts of love in this world than playing catch with dad. —B.L.
